title: Consumer Protection Act, 2019 replaced the 1986 Act

content.overview: Consumer Protection Act, 2019 replaced the 1986 Act. Governs consumers under S. 2(7) (excludes commercial purpose unless self-employment, Laxmi Engineering). Introduces Chapter VI Product Liability (strict liability on manufacturers, ss. 84-87), Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA), and 3-tier commissions (District up to ₹50L, State ₹50L–₹2Cr, National >₹2Cr). 2-year limitation (s. 69).

content.study:
Topic at a glance
The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (Act No. 35 of 2019, in force from 20 July 2020) repealed and replaced the three-decade-old Consumer Protection Act, 1986. Enacted to address modern market realities—including e-commerce, tele-shopping, digital contracts, algorithm-driven advertising, and multi-tier supply chains—the 2019 Act transforms consumer jurisprudence from the archaic common law rule of Caveat Emptor ("let the buyer beware") to Caveat Venditor ("let the seller beware"). It introduces a dedicated regulatory watchdog (the Central Consumer Protection Authority), a revolutionary statutory regime for Product Liability (Chapter VI), statutory recognition of mediation, and expanded consumer-centric territorial and pecuniary jurisdiction.

Jurisprudential roots & legislative purpose
In classical contract and tort law, individual consumers suffered from acute inequality of bargaining power when dealing with large corporate manufacturers, retailers, and service conglomerates. The doctrine of privity of contract and formalistic court delays often rendered common law remedies for defective goods or negligent services completely illusory.
The legislative purpose of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 is to provide simple, speedy, and inexpensive quasi-judicial redressal for consumer grievances, penalize unfair trade practices, and enforce non-negotiable statutory duties on manufacturers, sellers, e-commerce platforms, and endorsers.

Definition of "Consumer" (Section 2(7))
Under Section 2(7) of the 2019 Act, a "consumer" is any person who:
(a) Buys any goods for a consideration which has been paid or promised or partly paid and partly promised, or under any system of deferred payment; and includes any user of such goods other than the person who buys them when such use is made with the approval of the buyer;
(b) Hires or avails of any service for a consideration paid or promised, and includes any beneficiary of such service when availed with the approval of the hirer;
(c) The definition explicitly includes transactions through offline modes, direct selling, and e-commerce platforms.

The Commercial Purpose Exclusion:
The definition contains a vital statutory exception:
"Consumer does NOT include a person who obtains such goods for resale or for any commercial purpose."
- The Self-Employment Exception:
  The Explanation to Section 2(7) creates a crucial exception to the exclusion:
  "Commercial purpose does not include use by a person of goods bought and used by him and services availed by him exclusively for the purposes of earning his livelihood by means of self-employment."
- Landmark Authority — Laxmi Engineering Works v. P.S.G. Industrial Institute (1995) 3 SCC 583:
  The Supreme Court interpreted "commercial purpose" to mean an activity directed towards large-scale business with a view to generating substantial commercial profits. Where a person purchases machinery (e.g. a powerloom, tractor, photocopier, or diagnostic machine) to operate it personally or with family members to earn their livelihood, they remain a "consumer" entitled to statutory protection.

"Deficiency in Service" (Section 2(11))
"Deficiency" means any fault, imperfection, shortcoming, or inadequacy in the quality, nature, and manner of performance which is required to be maintained by or under any law for the time being in force, or has been undertaken to be performed by a person in pursuance of a contract or otherwise in relation to any service.
Scope of "Service" (Section 2(42)):
Includes banking, financing, insurance, transport, processing, supply of electrical or other energy, telecom, boarding or lodging, housing construction, entertainment, and amusement.
- Medical Services: In Indian Medical Association v. V.P. Shantha (1995) 6 SCC 651, the Supreme Court held that medical treatment rendered by medical practitioners and private hospitals for consideration falls squarely within the definition of "service." Patients can sue for medical negligence as a "deficiency of service" before Consumer Commissions.

Unfair Trade Practices & Misleading Advertisements (Section 2(47) & Section 21)
The 2019 Act broadens the definition of Unfair Trade Practices (UTPs) to include:
1. False representation regarding standard, quality, grade, or style of goods and services.
2. Refusal to issue a cash memo or bill.
3. Refusal to take back defective goods or refund money within the period stipulated.
4. Disclosure of consumer personal information in breach of privacy.
Misleading Advertisements & Celebrity Endorsers (Section 21):
The Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) can impose penalties up to ₹10 lakhs (and up to ₹50 lakhs for subsequent contraventions) on manufacturers, traders, and celebrity endorsers who make false claims without due diligence.

The Product Liability Framework (Chapter VI, Sections 82–87)
The most transformative introduction of the 2019 Act is Chapter VI, which creates a comprehensive strict liability statutory tort against manufacturers, service providers, and sellers for harm caused by defective products:
1. Product Manufacturer Liability (Section 84):
   Liable if the product contains a manufacturing defect, design defect, deviation from manufacturing specifications, does not conform to express warranty, or fails to contain adequate instructions or warnings for correct usage. Crucially, the manufacturer is liable even if they prove they were not negligent!
2. Product Service Provider Liability (Section 85):
   Liable if the service provided was faulty, imperfect, deficient, or failed to issue adequate warnings regarding safety hazards.
3. Product Seller Liability (Section 86):
   Although sellers are generally immune if the defect is internal to a sealed manufacturer product, a seller is liable if:
   - They exercised substantial control over designing, testing, or modifying the product.
   - They altered or modified the product and such modification caused the harm.
   - They failed to pass on the manufacturer’s express warnings.
4. Exceptions to Product Liability (Section 87):
   - The product was misused, altered, or modified by the consumer.
   - The danger was obvious or generally known to an ordinary user.
   - The product was purchased by an employer for use at the workplace and the employer failed to train the employee.

Three-Tier Quasi-Judicial Redressal Machinery
The 2019 Act establishes a three-tier hierarchy of Consumer Disputes Redressal Commissions:

| Forum | Composition | Pecuniary Jurisdiction (Amended 2021 Rules) |
|---|---|---|
| District Commission (s. 28) | President + not less than 2 Members | Value of goods/services paid does NOT exceed ₹50 Lakhs |
| State Commission (s. 42) | President + not less than 4 Members | Value of goods/services paid exceeds ₹50 Lakhs but does not exceed ₹2 Crores |
| National Commission - NCDRC (s. 53) | President + not less than 4 Members | Value of goods/services paid exceeds ₹2 Crores |

*Crucial Change from 1986 Act*: Under the 1986 Act, jurisdiction was calculated based on the "value of goods/services PLUS compensation claimed" (which allowed claimants to artificially inflate claims to leapfrog forums). Under the 2019 Act, jurisdiction is determined strictly by the actual "consideration paid."

Procedural & forum anchors (Senior Counsel Reference)
- Consumer-Friendly Territorial Jurisdiction (Section 34(2)(d)):
  Under the old 1986 Act, a consumer had to file where the opposite party resided or carried on business. Under Section 34(2)(d) of the 2019 Act, a complaint can be instituted where the complainant resides or personally works for gain. A consumer in Guwahati who buys a product online from a seller in Bengaluru can file the complaint in Guwahati!
- E-Filing & Video Conferencing: Section 35(1) enables online filing via the E-Daakhil portal and virtual hearings.
- Statutory Mediation (Chapter V): Commissions can refer disputes to attached Consumer Mediation Cells where there is an element of settlement.
- Limitation Period (Section 69):
  The complaint must be filed within **2 years** from the date on which the cause of action arose. Delay may be condoned if sufficient cause is shown with reasons recorded in writing.
- Appeals:
  - District Commission → State Commission: within 45 days (Section 41); requires mandatory deposit of 50% of the awarded amount.
  - State Commission → National Commission: within 30 days (Section 51).
  - National Commission → Supreme Court: within 30 days (Section 67).

Adversarial courtroom submissions
- Complainant / Consumer Submissions:
  1. Claimant is a bona fide consumer under Section 2(7) (goods/services purchased for consideration; self-employment exception applies if commercial use alleged).
  2. Clear deficiency in service under Section 2(11) or defect under Section 2(10).
  3. Invoke product liability under Section 84 against manufacturer for design/manufacturing flaw.
  4. Institute complaint within 2 years in the consumer’s home territorial commission under Section 34(2)(d).
- Opposite Party / Corporate Submissions:
  1. The complainant is not a consumer: goods were purchased for large-scale commercial generation of profits (Laxmi Engineering).
  2. The complaint is time-barred under Section 69 (exceeds 2 years without condonation).
  3. Product liability excluded under Section 87 due to consumer's unauthorized modification or misuse.
  4. The issue involves complex fraud requiring trial in a Civil Court rather than summary proceedings before Consumer Commissions.

Current-law close
The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 empowers Indian consumers through e-commerce coverage, product liability, consumer-friendly forum selection, and the CCPA. For litigation, always plead consideration paid to anchor pecuniary jurisdiction under the 2021 Rules and invoke Section 34(2)(d) for local jurisdiction.

examples.title: Example — Self-employment exception applied
examples.body: A qualified unemployed civil engineer purchases an earth-moving excavator on bank finance to personally operate it and clear construction debris to earn a livelihood for his family. The machine suffers hydraulic failure within three months. The manufacturer claims he is not a consumer because an excavator is commercial equipment. Held: Since the machine was purchased exclusively to earn a livelihood by means of self-employment, the self-employment exception under Section 2(7) applies. The engineer is a consumer (Laxmi Engineering Works v. P.S.G. Industrial Institute).

examples.title: Example — Commercial purpose exclusion (complaint barred)
examples.body: A multi-national software company operating three shifts with 500 employees purchases 100 air-conditioning units for its corporate headquarters. When several compressors fail, the company files a complaint before the State Commission claiming ₹40 lakhs damages. Held: The purchase was made to facilitate large-scale corporate commercial business and enhance profitability. It is a commercial purpose; the software corporation is not a "consumer" under Section 2(7) and must pursue ordinary remedies in Civil Court.

examples.title: Example — Product liability against manufacturer
examples.body: A consumer purchases a smartphone online. While recharging the device using the original charger provided in the box, the lithium battery explodes due to a defective internal separator, causing second-degree burns to the user’s hand and destroying furniture. Held: Under Section 84 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, the product manufacturer is strictly liable in product liability for a manufacturing and design defect, irrespective of whether the manufacturer exercised care in quality control.

hypotheticals.question: Does the District Consumer Commission at Ranchi have jurisdiction to entertain the complaint? Can an exclusive jurisdiction clause in an e-commerce agreement defeat the consumer’s statutory right under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019?
hypotheticals.analysis:
1. Territorial Jurisdiction under Section 34(2)(d):
Under Section 34(2)(d) of the 2019 Act, a consumer complaint may be instituted before a District Commission within the local limits of whose jurisdiction "the complainant resides or personally works for gain." This provision was explicitly enacted to liberate consumers from the hardship of travelling to distant corporate headquarters. Rina resides in Ranchi; hence, the District Commission at Ranchi possesses unequivocal statutory territorial jurisdiction.
2. Inefficacy of Exclusive Jurisdiction Clauses:
The Supreme Court in multiple rulings (e.g. Ethiopian Airlines v. Stic Travels, and M/s Zanders v. State) has affirmed that statutory provisions enacted for consumer welfare override private standard-form contractual forum selection clauses. An e-commerce platform cannot deprive a consumer of the statutory forum provided by Parliament under Section 34(2)(d).
3. Product Liability Claim:
Under Section 84, the manufacturer (SmartHome Appliances Ltd.) is strictly liable for manufacturing and design defects causing harm to property. Under Section 86, the e-commerce entity and vendor are also answerable as product sellers if they fail to pass on requisite relief.

misconceptions.trap: Believing that buying any machine or equipment disqualifies a buyer from being a consumer.
misconceptions.correction: Under the Explanation to Section 2(7) and the Laxmi Engineering ruling, if a person buys goods or machinery exclusively to earn their livelihood through personal self-employment, they remain a consumer.

misconceptions.trap: Assuming a consumer must travel to the manufacturer’s head office city to file a consumer complaint.
misconceptions.correction: Under Section 34(2)(d) of the 2019 Act, a consumer can file the complaint at their own place of residence or workplace, completely overriding corporate forum selection clauses.

cases.name: Laxmi Engineering Works v. P.S.G. Industrial Institute
cases.holding: Defined the scope of "commercial purpose" and the "self-employment exception". Held that a person purchasing machinery to operate it personally for earning a livelihood is a consumer, whereas commercial activity undertaken for large-scale profit generation is excluded.
cases.relevance: The foundational Supreme Court precedent interpreting the definition of consumer under Section 2(7).

cases.name: Indian Medical Association v. V.P. Shantha
cases.holding: Held that medical services rendered by medical practitioners and hospitals for consideration fall within the definition of "service". Patients can claim compensation for medical negligence before Consumer Forums.
cases.relevance: Brought the medical profession and healthcare institutions within the regulatory oversight of consumer law.

cases.name: Lucknow Development Authority v. M.K. Gupta
cases.holding: Held that statutory housing development authorities fall within the definition of service providers. Delay in handing over possession of flats or houses constitutes actionable deficiency in service.
cases.relevance: Extended consumer protection to real estate, housing construction, and statutory municipal boards.

questionsAndAnswers.question: Define a "Consumer" under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019. Explain the "commercial purpose" exclusion and the self-employment exception with reference to Laxmi Engineering Works v. P.S.G. Industrial Institute.
questionsAndAnswers.answer:
### 1. Introduction and Statutory Definition
The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 was enacted to protect the interests of consumers in an increasingly digital and market-driven economy.
Under Section 2(7) of the Act, a "consumer" is any person who:
1. Buys any goods for a consideration which has been paid, promised, partly paid, or under any deferred payment system, including any approved user of such goods.
2. Hires or avails of any service for a consideration paid, promised, or partly paid, including any approved beneficiary of such service.
3. The definition explicitly encompasses transactions conducted through offline modes, direct selling, tele-shopping, and e-commerce platforms.

### 2. The Commercial Purpose Exclusion
Section 2(7) explicitly provides that the term "consumer" does NOT include:
- A person who obtains goods for resale; or
- A person who obtains goods or avails services for any "commercial purpose."
The rationale is that the Act is designed to protect vulnerable end-users and consumers, not commercial traders who have the economic capacity and bargaining power to litigate in regular civil and commercial courts.

### 3. The Self-Employment Exception: Explanation to Section 2(7)
To prevent hardship to small entrepreneurs and self-employed individuals, the Explanation to Section 2(7) creates an express exception:
"Commercial purpose does not include use by a person of goods bought and used by him and services availed by him exclusively for the purposes of earning his livelihood by means of self-employment."

### 4. Judicial Interpretation: Laxmi Engineering Works v. P.S.G. Industrial Institute (1995) 3 SCC 583
The Supreme Court of India delivered the authoritative interpretation of this exception:
1. Facts: The appellant purchased a universal cylindrical grinding machine from the respondent for ₹21 lakhs to manufacture machine parts. The machine was defective, and the appellant filed a consumer complaint. The respondent contended that a high-capacity industrial machine was purchased for a commercial purpose.
2. Ruling of the Supreme Court:
   - "Commercial Purpose" implies an activity directed towards large-scale manufacture and trade with the primary objective of generating significant profits.
   - Whether a purchase is for a commercial purpose is a question of fact to be decided in each case.
   - If a person purchases a machine (e.g., a commercial printing machine, a taxi, a powerloom, or a tractor) to operate it personally for the purpose of earning their livelihood, they remain a "consumer."
   - If, however, the enterprise employs large-scale external labour and the purchaser does not operate the machine personally, it becomes a commercial venture outside the Act.

### 5. Conclusion
Section 2(7) strikes a balanced equilibrium: it excludes large-scale commercial entities seeking summary remedies, while safeguarding individual citizens and self-employed micro-entrepreneurs under the protective umbrella of the Consumer Protection Act.

questionsAndAnswers.question: Critically examine the major changes introduced by the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 over the 1986 Act. Explain the statutory framework governing Product Liability under Chapter VI and discuss the pecuniary and territorial jurisdiction of Consumer Commissions.
questionsAndAnswers.answer:
### 1. Abstract & Introduction
The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 marked a paradigm shift in Indian consumer welfare. By repealing the Consumer Protection Act, 1986, Parliament recognized that modern digital economies, dark patterns in advertising, e-commerce monopolies, and defective industrial manufacturing required a total structural overhaul. The 2019 Act introduced the Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA), a dedicated statutory chapter on Product Liability (Chapter VI), statutory consumer mediation, and revolutionary reforms in territorial and pecuniary jurisdiction.

### 2. Major Innovations of the 2019 Act over the 1986 Act
1. Inclusion of E-Commerce and Direct Selling:
   The 1986 Act did not contemplate electronic commerce. The 2019 Act explicitly brings e-commerce transactions, digital platforms, and online service providers within Section 2(7) and enacts the Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020.
2. Regulatory Watchdog — Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA):
   Under Chapter III, a proactive regulatory body (the CCPA) is established with an investigative wing headed by a Director-General. The CCPA has the power to initiate suo motu class-action investigations, order recall of unsafe goods, direct refund of prices, and impose heavy financial penalties on misleading advertisers and celebrity endorsers (Section 21).
3. Statutory Mediation:
   Chapter V integrates alternate dispute resolution by establishing Consumer Mediation Cells attached to every District, State, and National Commission.

### 3. The Product Liability Framework (Chapter VI, Sections 82–87)
Prior to 2019, an individual injured by a defective product had to institute a protracted civil suit in tort, proving fault and negligence under common law. Chapter VI codifies a strict liability statutory tort:
#### A. Liability of Product Manufacturer (Section 84):
A product manufacturer is liable in a product liability action if:
(a) The product contains a manufacturing defect;
(b) The product has a defective design;
(c) There is a deviation from manufacturing specifications;
(d) The product does not conform to an express warranty;
(e) The product fails to contain adequate instructions for correct use or warnings to prevent harm.
Crucially, under Section 84(2), the manufacturer is liable even if they prove they exercised due care and was not negligent!

#### B. Liability of Product Service Provider (Section 85):
A service provider is liable if the service provided was faulty, imperfect, or deficient in quality, or if it failed to provide adequate safety warnings.

#### C. Liability of Product Seller (Section 86):
Product sellers (including e-commerce platforms) are liable if they exercised substantial control over product design/testing, altered the product, or failed to pass on warnings.

#### D. Exceptions to Product Liability (Section 87):
Liability cannot be enforced if:
1. The consumer misused, altered, or modified the product.
2. The danger was obvious or generally known to a reasonable user.
3. The product was purchased by an employer for use by trained employees at a workplace.

### 4. Pecuniary Jurisdiction and the Shift to "Consideration Paid"
Under the 1986 Act, jurisdiction was determined by the value of goods/services PLUS the compensation claimed. Litigants routinely claimed exaggerated compensation of ₹1.01 Crore to directly approach the National Commission.
The 2019 Act, read with the Consumer Protection (Pecuniary Jurisdiction of the Commissions) Rules, 2021, rationalized jurisdiction based solely on the actual consideration paid:
1. District Commission (Section 28): Consideration paid does NOT exceed ₹50 Lakhs.
2. State Commission (Section 42): Consideration paid exceeds ₹50 Lakhs but does not exceed ₹2 Crores.
3. National Commission - NCDRC (Section 53): Consideration paid exceeds ₹2 Crores.

### 5. Consumer-Centric Territorial Jurisdiction: Section 34(2)(d)
Under Section 11 of the 1986 Act, a consumer had to institute the complaint where the opposite party resided or where the cause of action arose. This caused immense distress to consumers buying goods online from remote manufacturers.
Section 34(2)(d) of the 2019 Act enacts a progressive reform:
A complaint can now be filed within the local limits of the Commission where the complainant resides or personally works for gain.
Furthermore, Section 35(1) enables electronic filing of complaints through the E-Daakhil portal, and hearings can be conducted via video conferencing.

### 6. Limitation Period (Section 69)
The period of limitation for filing a consumer complaint before any Commission is **2 years** from the date on which the cause of action arose. Delay may be condoned by the Commission upon showing sufficient cause.

### 7. Conclusion
The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 represents a masterstroke of modern legislative drafting. By combining regulatory vigilance (CCPA) with strict Product Liability and empowering consumers to sue locally via digital e-filing, the Act ensures that corporate accountability and consumer dignity remain living realities in India.
questionsAndAnswers.explanation: Scoring Rubric: Allocate 4 marks for key innovations of the 2019 Act (CCPA, e-commerce, mediation), 5 marks for Chapter VI Product Liability (manufacturer, service provider, seller, exceptions), 4 marks for pecuniary (2021 rules) and territorial (s. 34(2)(d)) jurisdiction, and 3 marks for limitation (s. 69) and conclusion.

revisionPoints: Consumer Protection Act, 2019 in force from 20 July 2020; replaced the 1986 Act.
Consumer: Section 2(7) — excludes resale or commercial purpose, but includes self-employment exception (Laxmi Engineering).
Deficiency in service: Section 2(11) — includes medical services (IMA v. V.P. Shantha) and housing construction (LDA v. M.K. Gupta).
Product Liability: Chapter VI (Sections 82–87) — strict liability on manufacturers for design/manufacturing defects and failure to warn.
CCPA: Central Consumer Protection Authority (Chapter III) — regulatory watchdog with recall, investigation, and misleading ad penalty powers.
Pecuniary Jurisdiction (2021 Rules): District <= ₹50 Lakhs; State > ₹50 Lakhs to ₹2 Crores; National > ₹2 Crores (based strictly on consideration paid).
Territorial Jurisdiction: Section 34(2)(d) allows filing where complainant resides or works for gain.
Limitation: 2 years from date of cause of action under Section 69.
examTips: Always cite the 2021 Pecuniary Jurisdiction Rules in exams: District up to ₹50L, State up to ₹2Cr, National above ₹2Cr.
Emphasize that Section 34(2)(d) allows consumers to sue at their own residence, which is a major weapon against e-commerce companies.
Highlight that Product Liability under Section 84 does not require proof of negligence; it is strict statutory liability.
